narrative:
The model estimated a 56.3% chance that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. Because that is above the risk line used for admission, your application was denied. This was not a clear-cut failure prediction, but it was slightly more likely than not.

Of the factors that mattered most, your third-year class rank was by far the strongest and it pushed the prediction toward failure. Your decile was 1, meaning you were near the bottom of your class in Year 3, while accepted students averaged around decile 5.79. That gap was the main reason for the denial. The next most important factor was your LSAT. At 35.50 it was below the accepted-student average of 37.18, but in this prediction it leaned toward passing rather than failing. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.40 was the third most important factor; it was above the accepted average of 3.23 and also leaned toward passing. In other words, your GPA and LSAT were not what drove the rejection; your third-year academic standing did, and it outweighed those positive signals.

To move forward, focus on strengthening the weakest signal: take additional rigorous coursework or provide documented context for the low third-year rank, and ask recommenders to address your trajectory. Consider retaking the LSAT if you can improve meaningfully, and apply to programs with strong academic support and bar-passage resources. Seek admissions advising before reapplying.
